title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 130
paragraphs: When he was set in the midst of them, Darius asked him whether he understood the art; but he would not admit it, fearing that if he revealed what he was, he might lose forever the hope of returning to Hellas. It was clear to Darius, however, that he understood the art but was playing the ignorant, and he commanded those who had brought him to produce scourges and goads. Then he spoke out, saying that he did not understand the art precisely, but had kept company with a physician and had some slight knowledge of it. So when Darius had committed his case to him, by using Hellenic drugs and applying mild remedies after the former violent methods, he brought him to sleep and in a short time restored him completely, though the king had given up hope of being sound of foot again. On this Darius presented him with two pairs of golden fetters. Demokedes asked him whether he was deliberately giving him a double share of his suffering for making him well. Pleased with the remark, Darius sent him to visit his wives, and the eunuchs bringing him in told the women that this was the man who had restored the king's life. Each of them then plunged a cup into her gold-chest and gave Demokedes such an abundant gift that his servant, whose name was Skiton, following and picking up the coins that fell from the cups, gathered for himself a very large sum of gold.
